sections.text: 2 Preliminaries In this section, we formally define the task, introduce the models employed, and detail the mechanistic interpretability techniques used to dissect the internal location processing. 2.1 Task Formulation: Cell Location We focus on the fundamental operation of table understanding: locating the specific cell value given its corresponding row and column headers, which is a common subproblem of complex table-related tasks ( Pasupat and Liang, 2015 ) . We select cell location as it requires the model to not only perform semantic alignment but also to execute structural reasoning by navigating the coordinates ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . We first explore the atomic cell location task, and generalize our findings to the multi-cell location task. Formally, let a table T T be defined by a set of column headers 𝒞 = { c 1 , … , c C } \mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{C}\} and a set of row headers ℛ = { r 1 , … , r R } \mathcal{R}=\{r_{1},\dots,r_{R}\} , where row headers correspond to the unique identifiers in the primary key column. The cell value located at the intersection of row header r i r_{i} and column header h j h_{j} is denoted as v r i , h j v_{r_{i},h_{j}} . The table is serialized into a sequence of tokens x t ​ a ​ b ​ l ​ e x_{table} using a Markdown format with pipe delimiters (‘ | | ’) and newlines. The model is presented with a prompt x = [ D , x t ​ a ​ b ​ l ​ e , x q ​ u ​ e ​ r ​ y ] x=[D,x_{table},x_{query}] , where D D represents a one-shot demonstration. The query x q ​ u ​ e ​ r ​ y x_{query} is formulated as a natural language question that explicitly references a target row header constraint r ∈ ℛ r\in\mathcal{R} and a column header constraint c ∈ 𝒞 c\in\mathcal{C} . The objective is to generate the target token sequence y = v r , c y=v_{r,c} . To rigorously isolate structural reasoning from parametric knowledge memorization, we generate synthetic tables where cell values are randomly sampled from an entity pool, ensuring the model must rely solely on the provided context to align the requested headers with the table structure ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025a ) . Therefore, we construct a benchmark comprising 500 500 independent samples to evaluate the performance on this atomic cell location task, with details in Appendix B . 2.2 Models To ensure the generality of our findings, we conduct our analysis on a diverse set of decoder-only Transformer language models. Specifically, we utilize the Qwen series (including Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-32B) ( Yang et al., 2025a ) and the Llama series (including Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B) ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . These models employ Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) ( Su et al., 2024 ) and represent state-of-the-art open-weights architectures. We primarily report the results of Qwen3-4B as it achieves a high accuracy of 90 % 90\% on our benchmark. Our core findings consistently generalize across the other evaluated models, with detailed results and analysis in Appendix D . 2.3 Analytic Techniques To unravel the mechanism of table understanding, we employ a suite of mechanistic interpretability techniques. Activation Patching We employ Activation Patching to localize specific information flow within the model. Let 𝐡 t ( l ) ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the activation vector (residual stream) at layer l l and token position t t . To evaluate the causal contribution of a specific component, we perform an intervention by replacing its activation in a clean run (input x clean x_{\text{clean}} , target y y ) with the corresponding activation from a corrupted run (input x corrupt x_{\text{corrupt}} , foil y ′ y^{\prime} ). We consider two levels of granularity for patching, following previous works ( Wang et al., 2023b ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ) : • Layer-level Patching: We replace the residual stream 𝐡 t ( l ) \mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} across the specific token span t ∈ 𝒯 t\in\mathcal{T} to identify which layers and positions mediate the location process. • Head-level Patching: We replace the output of a specific attention head H ( l , a ) H^{(l,a)} (where a ∈ { 1 , … , A } a\in\{1,\dots,A\} denotes the head index) at the final input token position. This details the causal contributions of precise heads. To quantify the importance of the patched component, we use the Effect Score based on the Logit Difference (LD) ( Hong et al., 2025 ) . We define LD ​ ( x ) = logit ​ ( x ) y − logit ​ ( x ) y ′ \text{LD}(x)=\text{logit}(x)_{y}-\text{logit}(x)_{y^{\prime}} as the confidence margin between the target and the foil. The Effect Score is the normalized change in LD: Effect = LD patch − LD corrupt LD clean − LD corrupt \text{Effect}=\frac{\text{LD}_{\text{patch}}-\text{LD}_{\text{corrupt}}}{\text{LD}_{\text{clean}}-\text{LD}_{\text{corrupt}}} (1) where LD patch \text{LD}_{\text{patch}} denotes the logit difference after intervention. Scores near or above 1.0 1.0 indicate that the patched component is a pivotal mediator of the task. Linear Probing To investigate whether the model explicitly encodes geometric structures within its internal representations, we employ linear probing on the residual stream. For a dataset of N N samples, we train a linear regressor P P on the activations 𝐡 t ( l ) \mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} to predict the ground-truth geometric coordinates z ∈ { r i ​ d ​ x , c i ​ d ​ x } z\in\{r_{idx},c_{idx}\} . These represent the numerical row and column indices of the token in the table grid: z ^ = P ⁡ ( 𝐡 t ( l ) ) = 𝐖 p ​ 𝐡 t ( l ) + 𝐛 p \hat{z}=P(\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)})=\mathbf{W}_{p}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}+\mathbf{b}_{p} (2) where 𝐖 p ∈ ℝ 1 × d \mathbf{W}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d} and 𝐛 p ∈ ℝ \mathbf{b}_{p}\in\mathbb{R} are learnable parameters. We evaluate the probe using the coefficient of determination ( R 2 R^{2} score): R 2 = 1 − ∑ i = 1 N ( z i − z ^ i ) 2 ∑ i = 1 N ( z i − z ¯ ) 2 R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(z_{i}-\hat{z}_{i})^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(z_{i}-\bar{z})^{2}} (3) A high R 2 R^{2} score indicates that the model linearly encodes the structural coordinates of the table. We provide training and evaluation details in Appendix C.3 . Ablation Studies To verify the causal necessity of specific attention heads, we employ ablation techniques. The total output of the multi-head attention (MHA) block at layer l l and position t t is the aggregation of independent head outputs: MHA ​ ( 𝐡 t ( l ) ) = ∑ a = 1 A H t ( l , a ) \text{MHA}(\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)})=\sum_{a=1}^{A}H_{t}^{(l,a)} . We define a target set of heads ℋ a ​ b ​ l \mathcal{H}_{abl} to intervene upon. Zero Ablation explicitly removes the information flow from the target heads by forcing their output activations to zero ( Gould et al., 2024 ) : H ^ t ( l , a ) = 𝟎 , ∀ ( l , a ) ∈ ℋ a ​ b ​ l \hat{H}_{t}^{(l,a)}=\mathbf{0},\quad\forall(l,a)\in\mathcal{H}_{abl} (4) By measuring the change of outputs, we observe whether the targeted heads are necessary components for cell location.

3 The Three-Stage Information Flow of Table Understanding 3.1 Overview Figure 2 : Average column patching effect score across layers and token positions. Experimental Setup To map the information flow of table understanding, we employ activation patching on semantically segmented input sequences. Let ℐ q ​ ( r ) \mathcal{I}_{q}(r) and ℐ q ​ ( c ) \mathcal{I}_{q}(c) denote the query token spans for row and column constraints. Within the fixed table x t ​ a ​ b ​ l ​ e x_{table} , we define ℐ t ​ ( c ) \mathcal{I}_{t}(c) and ℐ t ​ ( r ) \mathcal{I}_{t}(r) as the token spans for the column header c c and row headers r r , and ℐ t ​ ( v r , c ) \mathcal{I}_{t}(v_{r,c}) as the span for the cell value located by r r and c c . We construct corrupted inputs x ′ x^{\prime} by altering the query constraints to a counterfactual column or row header, thereby shifting the target value location. We define two settings: • Column Patching: We replace the query column constraint c c with a counterfactual c ′ c^{\prime} . This shifts the target value indices from the correct span ℐ t ​ ( v r , c ) \mathcal{I}_{t}(v_{r,c}) to the counterfactual span ℐ t ​ ( v r , c ′ ) \mathcal{I}_{t}(v_{r,c^{\prime}}) . • Row Patching: We replace the query row constraint r r with r ′ r^{\prime} . This shifts the target indices to ℐ t ​ ( v r ′ , c ) \mathcal{I}_{t}(v_{r^{\prime},c}) . Figure 2 shows the Column Patching results, with detailed configurations and explanations of coordinates in Appendix C.1 . Given the symmetric spatiotemporal patterns, results of Row Patching are provided in Appendix C.1 . Analysis of Causal Dynamics Observing the distribution of Effect Scores across layers and positions reveals a sequential transition in causal importance, delineating the location process into three stages. Notably, this stratification reflects the concentration of the primary functional attention heads within these intervals but does not preclude the existence of a minority of relevant heads in other layers: 1. Stage I: Semantic Binding (Early Layers 1-16). Significant causal mass is concentrated on query constraints ( ℐ q ​ ( r ) , ℐ q ​ ( c ) \mathcal{I}_{q}(r),\mathcal{I}_{q}(c) ), whereas the impact on corresponding table headers ( ℐ t ​ ( r ) , ℐ t ​ ( c ) \mathcal{I}_{t}(r),\mathcal{I}_{t}(c) ) is comparatively marginal. 2. Stage II: Coordinate Localization (Middle Layers 17-23). The causal importance shift decisively from the headers to the target cell region ( ℐ t ​ ( v r , c ) \mathcal{I}_{t}(v_{r,c}) ). This transition suggests a functional shift from semantic matching to structural navigation, where the model utilizes the constraint header information to locate the specific intersection coordinates in the serialized table sequence. 3. Stage III: Information Propagation (Late Layers 24+). Interventions on all token positions yield negligible causal effects in this stage. This diminished sensitivity indicates that the answer v r , c v_{r,c} has already been resolved and encoded within the internal states. Consequently, the primary mechanism shifts from location to the propagation to the final token position for decoding. (a) Layer-wise Alignment (b) Ablation Error Flow Figure 3 : Analysis of semantic binding mechanisms. (a) Top-1 accuracy evaluated with cosine similarity between query constraints and all table headers across layers. (b) The impact of ablating row alignment heads by observing the changes of outputs. 3.2 Stage I: Semantic Binding To investigate the semantic binding of query constraints to table headers, we first analyze the geometric alignment of their internal representations. We compute the cosine similarity between hidden states of query constraints and candidate table headers at each layer, and evaluate using the top-1 accuracy, defined as the frequency with which the gold header exhibits the highest similarity score among all candidates. As illustrated in Figure 3(a) , the accuracy for both dimensions converges close to 1.0 1.0 in early layers, indicating that semantic mapping occurs well before information extraction. Notably, column headers exhibit tighter alignment than rows, suggesting easier binding, whereas row constraint resolution is strictly confined to the initial layers. We further explore the causal mechanism via attention ablation. We identify specialized alignment heads, which exhibit preferential attention from query constraints to target table headers, with detailed setup in Appendix C.2 . In Figure 3(b) , only the exact flow represents correct predictions, while other flows ar error types. Zero-ablating the top-20 of row alignment heads ( 95 % 95\% in layers 1-16) triggers a catastrophic performance collapse from 94.4 % 94.4\% to 5.2 % 5.2\% . Conversely, ablating the top-20 column alignment heads or a random selection of heads results in marginal performance degradations of 6.6 % 6.6\% and 13.8 % 13.8\% , respectively. Notably, random head ablation results in a mere 11.0 % 11.0\% wrong row (the output in the correct column but error row) rate, which is significantly lower than 29.4 % 29.4\% with row alignment heads, confirming that the identified heads are responsible for binding row header semantic information. Therefore, row grounding necessitates explicit semantic attention, column localization operates independently of strong attention weights, suggesting a process driven by signals beyond semantic alignment. Figure 4 : Visualization of the geometric interaction score S j , l S_{j,l} in coordinate-encoding heads. The heatmap illustrates the dot product between column-averaged query vectors ( q ¯ j \bar{q}_{j} ) and key vectors ( k ¯ l \bar{k}_{l} ) after injecting RoPE corresponding to their column indices. 3.3 Stage II: Coordinate Localization Following semantic alignment, the model transitions to locating the geometric coordinates of the target cell. Specifically, once the row header is identified, the model must locate the target cell corresponding to the correct column header. To determine whether the model relies on structural geometry rather than semantic matching for this stage, we conduct the analysis of the Query-Key interactions. We investigate whether specific attention heads explicitly encode column indices via RoPE. We extract query and key vectors from the residual stream and average them based on their respective column indices to eliminate specific semantic content. Let q ¯ j \bar{q}_{j} denote the average query vector across column constraints where the target is the j j -th column, and k ¯ l \bar{k}_{l} denote the average key vector for table cells located in the l l -th column. We artificially inject positional information using these column indices and compute the geometric interaction score S j , l S_{j,l} as: S j , l = RoPE ​ ( q ¯ j , j ) T ​ RoPE ​ ( k ¯ l , l ) S_{j,l}=\text{RoPE}(\bar{q}_{j},j)^{T}\text{RoPE}(\bar{k}_{l},l) (5) where RoPE ​ ( ⋅ , p ) \text{RoPE}(\cdot,p) represents the rotary embedding operation at position index p p . We select the top 20 attention heads ( 90 % 90\% in layers 17-23) that maximize the contrast between diagonal ( j = l j=l ) and off-diagonal ( j ≠ l j\neq l ) interaction scores. We term these coordinate-encoding heads . Figure 4 exhibits a distinct diagonal pattern where S j , l S_{j,l} is maximized significantly when the query target index matches the key column index. This geometric alignment provides strong evidence that the model utilizes a structural navigation mechanism in the middle layers. This suggests that the learned projections are optimized to leverage RoPE properties, facilitating an alignment mechanism based on the relative column indices of the query and the target cell. This confirms that the model abandons semantic matching in this stage effectively treating the serialized table as a coordinate system to locate the correct value. Figure 5 : Effect Scores of patching attention heads at the last token position. The red boxes highlight heads that exhibit positive Effect Scores and attention the target cell significantly. 3.4 Stage III: Information Propagation We investigate the final stage where the model moves the identified content to the last token position for generation. Therefore, we execute activation patching at the position of the last token. To isolate the mechanism responsible for location, we maintain the table context x t ​ a ​ b ​ l ​ e x_{table} constant and modify the query x q ​ u ​ e ​ r ​ y x_{query} to target a distinct row header r ′ r^{\prime} and column header c ′ c^{\prime} . We compute the Effect Score for each attention head to quantify its contribution to predicting the correct target y y versus y ′ y^{\prime} . Figure 5 presents the Effect Scores across all layers and heads at the final input token position. We observe that attention heads exhibiting an Effect Score greater than zero become densely distributed starting from Layer 24. To discern the functional mechanism of these high-scoring components we analyze their attention distribution over the input sequence. We discover that the three attention heads highlighted by red boxes allocate significant attention weights to the target cell token v r , c v_{r,c} in over 70 % 70\% of the samples compared to other context tokens. This behavior characterizes them as information mover heads that propagate the stored value from the resolved coordinates to the residual stream of the final token for decoding.

4 Implicit Coordinate System via Delimiter Counting Having established that the model performs coordinate localization in the middle layers, we now investigate the precise mechanism by which these coordinates are constructed. We hypothesize that the model constructs an implicit coordinate system by linearly scanning the serialized sequence. Figure 6 : R 2 R^{2} of column probes and row probes trained for cells and delimiters across layers. (a) Column prob (b) Row prob Figure 7 : The probe’s predicted column and row indices (blue) versus ground truth (orange) across the linearized table cells at layer 17. 4.1 Representations of Column and Row Indices To verify the existence of internal coordinate representations, we analyze the performance of the linear probes trained on the residual stream activations across different layers. We train independent probes to predict the column index c i ​ d ​ x c_{idx} and row index r i ​ d ​ x r_{idx} for every cell token in the table sequence x t ​ a ​ b ​ l ​ e x_{table} at each layer. We show the average R 2 R^{2} across the tokens to observe the geometric structure representations across layers in Figure 6 . As indicated by the dashed lines, R 2 R^{2} for both column and row probes stabilizes between layers 17 and 23, achieving peak values of 0.954 0.954 and 0.809 0.809 at layer 17. Notably, the column probes exhibit superior performance compared to row probes, corroborating that the model utilizes column indices as its primary navigation mechanism, while treating row positions as secondary features derived cumulatively from row boundaries (implying a reliance on semantic content for row grounding). Figure 7 illustrates the behavior of the predicted column indices and row indices. We observe a distinct sawtooth pattern where the predicted column index increases linearly within each row. Crucially, as the model encounters the row boundary, the predicted column index sharply resets to zero before resuming its linear ascent for the subsequent row. This indicates that the model tracks column index via a counter that resets upon detecting a row delimiter. In contrast, the row index representation manifests as a stepwise function . The predicted row value remains relatively constant throughout the tokens of a single row and undergoes a discrete increment only when the sequence transitions to the next line. Furthermore, the predicted indices increasingly diverge from the ground truth as the row and column counts grow, indicating that the model’s capacity for table understanding degrades with increasing table dimensions. 4.2 Role of Delimiters The sawtooth pattern observed above implies that the model relies on specific tokens to govern its counting mechanism. We posit that the pipe delimiter (‘ | | ’) serves as the fundamental trigger for this incremental counting process. Probe Comparison To disentangle whether coordinate information is intrinsic to cell content or anchored to structural delimiters, we analyze the layer-wise evolution of probe performance. While both delimiter and cell-based probes eventually reach comparable peak R 2 R^{2} values in deeper layers, their trajectory differs significantly (Figure 6 ). Probes trained on delimiter tokens exhibit robust linear separability ( R 2 > 0.95 R^{2}>0.95 ) immediately in the early layers. In contrast, cell content probes show a marked latency, stabilizing at high accuracy only after Layer 15. This performance gap in the initial 23 layers suggests a hierarchical information flow: the model first resolves coordinate states at the delimiter positions and subsequently propagates this positional information to the constituent cell tokens. Thus, the delimiter acts not merely as a separator, but as the primary synchronization signal for the model’s internal coordinate system. We also present the results of using other tabular formats with different delimiters in Appendix C.4 . Table 1: Effect Scores of activation patching on top 20 coordinate-encoding heads, which are selected by the R 2 R^{2} of probes trained on cells and delimiters, respectively. Head Function Probing Position Cell Delimiter Row Index Heads 0.006 0.006 0.527 0.527 Column Index Heads 0.025 0.025 0.958 0.958 Activation Patching To corroborate the hypothesis that coordinate states originate at delimiters and subsequently propagate to cells, we perform a targeted causal intervention. We identify the top-20 attention heads based on R 2 R^{2} of probes for row and column indices at both cell and delimiter positions. We then construct counterfactual inputs by swapping rows or columns to shift the geometric coordinates of the target cell while keeping the query constant. By patching the activations of these specific heads from the original to the swapped sequence at the target cell position, we measure their causal contribution via the Effect Score. Table 1 summarizes the results, revealing a clear causal hierarchy that mirrors our probing observations. Interventions on heads associated with cell content yield negligible Effect Scores ( 0.006 0.006 for rows, 0.025 0.025 for columns). This indicates that although cell tokens eventually encode positional information (as shown by late-layer probe accuracy in Figure 6 ), they are downstream recipients rather than drivers of the counting mechanism. In contrast, heads operating at delimiter positions demonstrate decisive causal control. The column index heads at delimiters achieve a near-perfect Effect Score of 0.958 0.958 , with row heads reaching 0.527 0.527 . These findings confirm that the delimiter serves as the causal origin of the coordinate system, actively driving the indexing process before the state is synchronized to the cell content. We also show the experiments of noise intervention in Appendix C.5 . Synthesizing findings from above, we conclude that the model locate cells by simulating a discrete ordinal coordinate system. This system is strictly ordinal: the model resolves column indices through the sequential accumulation of delimiter synchronization signals. Similarly, row indices are updated via discrete state transitions at row boundaries. Then the model propagates the tabular indices to the constituent cell tokens. This mechanism ensures that the internal representation is driven exclusively by the logical structure of the input rather than semantic length.

5 The Linear Geometry of Tabular Indices In this section, we investigate the geometric properties of column index representation. We hypothesize that the model represents column indices within a structured linear subspace governed by translation invariance and additivity. We show the detailed experiment setup in Appendix C.6 . 5.1 Steering with Unit Shift Vectors To characterize the geometric regularity and translation invariance of the column representation, we derive a global unit shift vector v → u ​ n ​ i ​ t \vec{v}_{unit} by averaging the mean activation differences between adjacent column header tokens in x t ​ a ​ b ​ l ​ e x_{table} across layers 17-23. We then perform steering interventions by modifying the target activation 𝐡 \mathbf{h} as 𝐡 ~ = 𝐡 + k ⋅ α ⋅ v → u ​ n ​ i ​ t \tilde{\mathbf{h}}=\mathbf{h}+k\cdot\alpha\cdot\vec{v}_{unit} where k ∈ ℤ k\in\mathbb{Z} is an integer representing the desired column shift and α \alpha is a steering coefficient. Figure 8 : Effect Scores resulting from injecting the unit shift vector scaled by integer factors k k . The positive integers denote rightward shifts and negative integers denote leftward shifts. Figure 8 illustrates the Effect Score across different integer shifts k k , which provides strong evidence for the linearity of the column representation. We observe that multiplying the unit shift vector by k k consistently steers the model to focus on the column located k k steps. This suggests that the model locates the cell by aligning its column position with that of the target column header, and encodes column positions as equidistant states along a specific direction in the activation space. The ability to traverse multiple columns by scaling a single vector confirms that the internal coordinate system possesses a robust linear structure. 5.2 Compositionality of Column Vectors We further investigate the additive compositionality of the representation space. If the subspace is truly linear, the vector required to shift attention by k k columns should be decomposable: the sum of two vectors shifting by a a and b b columns should be functionally equivalent to a single shift of a + b = k a+b=k columns. We define the composite vector v → c ​ o ​ m ​ p = v → a + v → b \vec{v}_{comp}=\vec{v}_{a}+\vec{v}_{b} and compare its steering effect against the baseline vector v → k \vec{v}_{k} , which is directly extracted from columns separated by distance k k . We conduct experiments for various target offsets k k using multiple combinations of constituent shifts a a and b b drawn from the range [ − 6 , 6 ] [-6,6] . We evaluate the interventions using the Effect Score. Figure 9 : Comparison of Effect Scores between Baseline Vectors (red stars) and Composite Vectors (blue dots). The Baseline Vector is the shift vector directly extracted for target shift k k . The Composite Vectors are formed by summing v → a + v → b \vec{v}_{a}+\vec{v}_{b} such that a + b = k a+b=k . Figure 9 shows the results of baseline and composite vectors, with details in Appendix C.6 . The alignment between the red baseline stars and the blue composite dots indicates a high degree of linearity. For a target shift of k = 4 k=4 the baseline vector achieves an Effect Score of 1.079 1.079 , and the composite vectors formed by linear combinations such as 1 + 3 1+3 yield comparable Effect Scores of 1.169 1.169 . This pattern holds for negative shifts as well where a target of k = − 4 k=-4 with a baseline score of 0.367 0.367 is closely matched by the combination of − 2 + ( − 2 ) -2+(-2) yielding 0.357 0.357 . The results confirm that the column indices form a linear subspace where vector addition preserves the relative spatial geometry.

6 Generalization to Multi-Cell Location 6.1 Experimental Setup To evaluate the generalization of the internal pipeline, we extend the atomic cell location task to multi-cell location scenarios. We construct two distinct benchmarks each consisting of 500 500 samples (details in Appendix B ). These benchmarks retain the same tables with the benchmark of the atomic cell location task, with the modifications applied solely to the natural language questions. In the Multi-Row setting the query x q ​ u ​ e ​ r ​ y x_{query} explicitly references a subset of target row headers ℛ s ​ u ​ b ⊂ ℛ \mathcal{R}_{sub}\subset\mathcal{R} and a single target column header c ∈ 𝒞 c\in\mathcal{C} . The objective is to locate the set of values { v r , c ∣ r ∈ ℛ s ​ u ​ b } \{v_{r,c}\mid r\in\mathcal{R}_{sub}\} corresponding to the intersection of the specified rows and the target column. In the Multi-Column setting the query specifies a single row header r ∈ ℛ r\in\mathcal{R} and a subset of target column headers 𝒞 s ​ u ​ b ⊂ 𝒞 \mathcal{C}_{sub}\subset\mathcal{C} requiring the location of values { v r , c ∣ c ∈ 𝒞 s ​ u ​ b } \{v_{r,c}\mid c\in\mathcal{C}_{sub}\} . This design allows us to investigate whether the model resolves multiple constraints through sequential processing or by parallelizing the semantic binding and coordinate localization mechanisms. (a) Error distribution post-ablation. (b) Multi-threaded coordinate localization. Figure 10 : Mechanistic analysis on the multi-cell location task. (a) illustrates the impact of ablating the row alignment heads identified in Stage I on multi-row queries. (b) depicts the Query-Key interaction scores for the top-20 coordinate-encoding heads from Stage II on multi-column queries. 6.2 Parallel Semantic Binding We investigate whether the semantic binding mechanism identified in the atomic cell location task generalizes to multi-row scenarios. We hypothesize that the model reuses the specifically identified row alignment heads from Stage I (§ 3.2 ) to process multiple constraints in parallel rather than instantiating distinct mechanisms. Specifically, this parallelism is inherent to the self-attention mechanism, where these heads compute binding scores for all query constraints concurrently across the sequence dimension. To verify this we perform an ablation study where we zero-ablate the top-20 row alignment heads, which are discovered in the atomic cell location task, during the processing of multi-row queries and observe the changes of model outputs. Figure 10(a) visualizes the distribution of error types following the ablation. The Sankey diagram reveals a catastrophic collapse in performance ( 81.8 % → 0.4 % 81.8\%\to 0.4\% ). Specifically, 38.4 % 38.4\% of samples shifting from exact matches to the wrong row or row header (directly outputting the row headers in the query) error categories. This specific failure mode mirrors the degradation observed in the atomic cell location setting, confirming that the model relies on the identical set of functional components to resolve multiple semantic targets. This demonstrates that the model does not resort to an iterative or multi-step reasoning strategy; instead, it possesses the capacity for parallel execution, where the row alignment operator is instantiated across representation sites within the latency of a single forward pass. 6.3 Multi-Threaded Coordinate Localization We subsequently examine the coordinate localization mechanism for multi-column queries. Crucially, we utilize the top-20 coordinate-encoding heads previously identified in the atomic cell location analysis (Stage II in § 3.3 ) to explore the model’s behavior in multi-column settings. We apply the RoPE-based interaction metric to the heads to compute the geometric interaction scores between the query column representations and the key vectors of the table columns. Figure 10(b) displays the average interaction scores for these specific top-20 coordinate-encoding heads. The heatmap reveals that the attention patterns of these heads exhibit strong positive interaction scores on the indices that correspond to all queried columns simultaneously. The preservation of the diagonal alignment pattern across multiple targets confirms that the coordinate-encoding heads are not limited to single-state tracking. This implies that the linear coordinate system operates as a superposition-ready vector space, where the same set of attention heads can calculate geometric offsets for distinct targets in parallel and locate the corresponding values in a single forward pass.
